captions: Let's break down the Horizon Industrial Parks I-P-O —
a two thousand six hundred crore mainboard issue,
and one of the biggest of this week.
It's a Blackstone-backed warehousing and industrial real-estate company.
We'll cover what it does, its full financials —
income statement, balance sheet and cash flow —
where the money goes, how it's valued,
and whether it fits you.
This is education, not investment advice.
So what does Horizon do?
It owns and leases warehousing and industrial parks —
the grade-A sheds and logistics buildings that e-commerce,
manufacturers and third-party logistics firms rent.
It's large: about forty-five assets across ten cities,
roughly fifty-eight million square feet of leasable space.
And it's controlled by Blackstone,
the global real-estate giant,
with about an eighty-nine percent stake.
It rides India's warehousing and supply-chain boom —
but note, it's still loss-making, as we'll see.
Now the financials — and here's the tension.
Revenue grew fast — up seventy-seven percent,
to about six hundred and ninety-one crore.
But the company is loss-making: a net loss of about two hundred and four crore in FY twenty twenty-six,
and that loss actually widened from a hundred and seventy-nine crore the year before.
And it's heavily leveraged —
total borrowings near six thousand eight hundred and eighty-four crore.
So: strong top-line growth, but red ink and a lot of debt.
Let's put all three statements together.
The income statement shows revenue near six hundred and ninety-one crore,
but a net loss of about two hundred and four crore that's widening.
The balance sheet is the worry —
nearly six thousand nine hundred crore of borrowings against fifty-eight million square feet of assets.
On the cash-flow side,
the I-P-O brings in two thousand six hundred crore fresh,
and about two thousand two hundred and fifty crore of that repays debt.
The public summaries don't publish the full operating cash-flow line —
for that, you read the R-H-P.
Where does your money go?
And on structure, Horizon scores well.
The entire two thousand six hundred crore is a fresh issue —
one hundred percent.
There is no Offer for Sale,
which means Blackstone and the other owners are not cashing out; every rupee goes into the company.
That's the good kind of structure.
The catch, of course, is what the money is for —
mostly paying down that big pile of debt.
What does the fresh money fund?
Overwhelmingly, debt repayment —
about two thousand two hundred and fifty crore,
the lion's share, repays borrowings.
So this is primarily a balance-sheet clean-up,
not an expansion war-chest.
It cuts interest costs — genuinely helpful —
but even afterwards, sizeable debt remains.
The small remainder goes to general corporate purposes.
So how is it priced against rivals?
This is where you must be careful.
Because it's loss-making, the P/E ratio can't be used —
there are no earnings to divide by.
So look at sales: at the top of the band,
Horizon is valued near seventeen thousand three hundred crore —
about twenty-five times its revenue.
That is a rich price for a company still in the red.
And don't confuse it with the listed warehousing REITs like Embassy,
Nexus or Mindspace —
those are yield instruments that pay out rent.
Horizon is an operating company that isn't yet profitable.
So — should you subscribe?
The strengths are real — the whole issue is fresh money,
it's backed by Blackstone,
it owns a large fifty-eight-million-square-foot platform,
and revenue is growing over seventy-seven percent on a genuine warehousing boom.
But the watch-outs are serious — the company is loss-making,
and the loss is widening; it carries nearly six thousand nine hundred crore of debt,
still high even after the I-P-O; and it's priced at about twenty-five times sales for that red ink.
The takeaway — a marquee-backed growth platform,
but a loss-making, debt-heavy one at a full price.
Only you can decide if the story is worth the risk.
Finally — how do you apply, and how much?
Retail investors bid up to two lakh for a thirty-five percent quota,
with allotment by lottery if oversubscribed.
H-N-Is bid above two lakh for a fifteen percent quota.
For Horizon, at a fifty-seven to sixty rupee band,
one lot works out to about fifteen thousand rupees —
your minimum.
Track the live subscription on the N-S-E and B-S-E I-P-O pages,
Chittorgarh, Moneycontrol, or your broker app.
Let's recap Horizon Industrial Parks.
A Blackstone-backed warehousing and industrial-parks company —
large, national,
and growing revenue over seventy-seven percent.
The issue is one hundred percent fresh, which is good —
but the money mostly repays a heavy debt load near six thousand nine hundred crore.
It's still loss-making, so the P/E doesn't apply,
and at about twenty-five times sales it's richly priced.
The retail minimum is about fifteen thousand rupees.
